analysis.one_liner: Phases out the federal program allowing employers to pay disabled workers below minimum wage.
analysis.headline: The bill to phase out the subminimum wage for workers with disabilities drew 7 cosponsors but never received a vote in the Senate committee or on the floor before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law lets employers with a special certificate pay workers with disabilities less than the minimum wage, sometimes just pennies an hour. This bill would raise those wages to the full federal minimum over six years, ban any new certificates, and offer hundreds of millions in grants to help employers convert to jobs that pay full wages alongside other services. It never received so much as a committee vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers with disabilities who are currently paid below the federal minimum wage under section 14(c) certificates. It would also benefit the service providers and state agencies that support them into competitive jobs, through grants to retool programs.

how_it_helps.text: The bill raises the wage floor for certificate holders in steps — 50% of the federal minimum after six months, 60% after two years, and so on up to 100% at the end of six years — and then makes every special certificate legally void.
It immediately bars the Labor Department from issuing any new special certificate to employers that do not already hold one, stopping the program from growing.

It authorizes $300 million in grants: $2–10 million per state and $100,000–500,000 per employer to convert businesses from segregated subminimum-wage workshops to competitive integrated employment with wraparound services.
It funds technical assistance through a nonprofit and an independent multi-year evaluation of what happens to workers' wages and employment during the transition.

analysis.who_pays: Employers holding 14(c) certificates — largely nonprofit and state-affiliated disability service providers running sheltered workshops — lose the ability to pay below minimum wage, and taxpayers fund the $300 million in transition grants.

drawbacks.text: Some families and providers argued that ending subminimum certificates could leave workers with the most significant disabilities without any job at all if employers stop offering those positions rather than pay full wages. The bill tried to blunt this with grants, technical assistance, and a grandfather clause letting anyone employed under a certificate as of June 4, 1997 stay in their existing setting for life.

The transition would cost public money — $300 million authorized for fiscal years 2020 through 2025 — on top of state Medicaid and vocational-rehabilitation spending that the bill requires states to align.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill gives a real pay raise to one of the lowest-paid groups in the workforce, and its six-year ramp, transition grants, and grandfather clause show a serious attempt to handle the objection that some workers could lose their placements. The main risk is execution: if competitive jobs and support services do not materialize fast enough, some workers could end up with neither a workshop job nor a community one. The grants were designed to prevent that, but success depended on funding and state follow-through.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended, with no hearing, no markup, and no vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Bob Casey introduced the bill on January 29, 2019, joined by Sen. Chris Van Hollen, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
Seven senators cosponsored the bill — six Democrats and one Independent.
The committee took no further action; the bill's entire action history is introduction and referral, and it never advanced in the 116th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers holding 14(c) certificates kept the legal ability to pay disabled workers below the federal minimum wage, since the program was never phased out. The workers affected by the certificates gained nothing.

against.name: Sheltered workshop operators and disability service providers holding 14(c) certificates
against.role: Employers whose business model depends on paying disabled workers below minimum wage

sides.party_line_note: Every cosponsor was a Democrat or the chamber's Independent; no Republicans signed on, and the Republican-chaired committee never moved the bill.

industries.industry: Disability service providers holding 14(c) certificates (sheltered workshop operators)
industries.note: The bill phases out their legal ability to pay workers with disabilities less than the federal minimum wage over six years and voids the certificates at the end, eliminating a below-minimum-wage labor model. It offers transition grants to soften the blow, but their core cost structure changes permanently.

State and employer grants fund converting programs to competitive integrated employment with wraparound services, and a nonprofit technical-assistance grant creates new work in helping employers make the switch.
States must make multiple agencies partners in the transition and eventually certify that no certificate employment remains, but they receive up to $10 million each to fund it.
